name: Tara Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy rice, flour, cooking oil, tinned tomatoes and frozen goods for Hartley Family Wholesale, which has been supplying corner shops and small restaurants around Eastgate for 40 years. I'm in by 6:30, because the shopkeepers ring in early. I check the stock board, call the importers and the mills, and settle prices with men who've known me since I started at 23. It wears me out in Ramadan and Diwali weeks, when everyone orders three times the usual and wants it yesterday, but I wouldn't swap it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I'm not surprised, because a computer has never carried a sack of rice or been woken at five by a shopkeeper. At the temple, we'd laugh about it. Online I'd say nothing, I don't use it for opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel vindicated. I've seen new systems promise everything, and the real work is still people trusting people. Mr Hartley, the owner, says it's a family firm and I believe him, so I don't worry about my place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd keep ringing my importers, keep sending the orders by hand, and keep taking the Friday evening shift at the community kitchen. We'd keep paying 500 extra on the mortgage, and I'd put a little into Aarav's and Diya's school fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. A bit tired, since the mortgage and two growing children keep us busy, but nothing about this picture would keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the real work is people trusting people. Can you give me an example from last year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In March, a flour mill had a fire and couldn't deliver. I rang the owner of another mill, a man I'd bought from for ten years, and he found us 20 tonnes in two days. A computer could have found the supplier, but it couldn't have called in a favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that already worries you about the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big supermarket chains. They're buying direct and the corner shops are closing one by one. If our customers go, it won't matter what a computer does.

say: I'd say a computer has never carried a **sack of rice** or been woken at five by a shopkeeper.
Online I'd say nothing, since I don't use it for opinions.
think: I'd feel **vindicated**: the real work is still people trusting people.
The owner calls it a family firm, so I don't worry about my place.
do: Keep ringing my **importers** and sending orders by hand.
Keep the Friday evening shift at the **community kitchen**.
Pay **500 extra** on the mortgage and add to the children's school fund.
feel: **Settled, a bit tired**, since the mortgage and two children keep us busy.
S0.quote: A computer could have found the supplier, but it couldn't have called in a favour.
fieldNote: Tara's calm comes from **relationships** and the family-firm culture, not from any interest in the technology.
Her real worry is supermarket chains buying direct and corner-shop customers closing.
Never uses AI tools, and is confident that trust-based buying survives.

steps.text: Keep ringing the importers and mills every morning
Pay 500 extra a month on the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's wait and see what actually works, and keep the shopkeepers' orders done by people who know them. At the temple I'd say people should be ready for change, but not scared. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be uneasy. A lot of what I do is on that list, the checking, planning and buying. Mr Hartley says the firm looks after its own, but his sons are talking about software, and I know how that goes when the accounts get tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the training the company offers, though I'd drag my feet. I'd make sure the shopkeepers still have a name and a number to call at Hartley, mine. I'd put 200 more a month into savings, and I'd speak to my brother-in-law about work at his import business in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little frightened of being left behind. I'm not stupid, I just never took to those things, and I'm 43 with two children to feed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drag your feet. What would help you actually learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone patient, sitting next to me for an hour a week, showing me on my own orders instead of a slide deck. If Priya from accounts did that, I'd learn faster. I learn from people, not screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the shopkeepers feel about ordering through software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of the older ones would hate it. They want to hear my voice and argue about price. If the firm switches them all to an app, some will go elsewhere, and that's a risk the owner's sons don't see yet.

say: I'd say let's **wait and see** what actually works and keep orders with people who know the shopkeepers.
At the temple I'd say people should be ready for change, not scared.
think: Much of what I do is on that list, so I'm **uneasy**.
The owner says the firm looks after its own, but his sons are talking about **software**.
do: Go to the company **training**, though reluctantly.
Make sure shopkeepers keep a **name and number** at Hartley, mine.
Put **200 more a month** into savings and talk to my brother-in-law about work.
feel: **A little frightened** of being left behind, with two children to feed.
S1.quote: I learn from people, not screens.
fieldNote: Tara's resistance is a **learning style**: she learns from patient people, not slides or screens.
Believes older shopkeepers will leave if the firm forces them onto an app.
Hedges with her brother-in-law's import business while trusting the family owner.

steps.text: Go to the company training and ask for a patient helper
Keep my name and number as the shopkeepers' contact
Put 200 more a month into savings
Talk to my brother-in-law about work at his import business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to sit down as a family firm and decide how to protect our people, before the machines decide. At the temple I'd ask people to pray and also to prepare, because God helps those who help themselves. Online, no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone. Two years isn't time for someone who's never learned these things to start again. The drivers and the warehouse staff have three more years, which is a mercy, but I sit at a desk and my job is all thinking and talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with my husband Vikram that same week and cut 700 a month, no holidays, no new car. I'd talk to my brother-in-law and my cousin about starting a small catering and food-supply business, using my contacts. And I'd ask the temple and my sister about help for the children if we needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd pray more than usual, and I'd be short with the children, which I'd hate. Eight months of savings sounds like a lot, until I imagine paying the mortgage out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask family and the temple for help. Is that easy for you to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it's hard. I was raised that you pay your own way and don't ask, but I'd do it for my children. And I'd give back double when I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Aarav and Diya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that Mum's work is changing, that we have each other, and that we will be careful with money. I'd say we'd do the Saturday food-box shifts together so they see that we help others, even when we're worried.

say: I'd say the family firm should decide how to protect its **people** before machines decide.
At the temple I'd ask people to pray and also to prepare.
think: My job is **gone**, and two years is too short for me to start again.
The drivers get three more years, which is a **mercy**.
do: Cut **700 a month** with my husband Vikram and skip holidays and a new car.
Start a small **food-supply business** with my cousin using my importer contacts.
Ask my sister and the temple for **help** with the children if needed.
feel: **Frightened**: I'd pray more and be short with the children.
S2.quote: I was raised that you pay your own way and don't ask, but I'd do it for my children.
fieldNote: Tara expects to lose her desk job and asks for **community help**, which goes against her upbringing.
Plans a small food-supply business with her cousin, using decades of importer contacts.
Wants her children to see her help others through Saturday food boxes even when worried.

steps.text: Cut 700 a month with Vikram and skip holidays
Start a small food-supply business with my cousin
Ask my sister and the temple for help with the children
Ask the owner for a transition plan for desk staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is time to prepare, and I'd offer to train younger staff in how to talk to customers and mills. At the temple I'd say work hard and save. Online I'd say nothing, but I'd show my children how to look things up carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I have time to adjust, but I wouldn't know to what. I'd be 48, with Aarav near the end of school, and I'd worry about paying for his studies. The mortgage would be half done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to build the side business, selling rice and spices to a few restaurants, on top of my job. I'd take a bookkeeping course, because every business needs one. And I'd save 600 a month and make sure Vikram's job and mine aren't in the same basket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit steadier than 2028. Five years is enough to learn a new thing slowly. I'm not quick with new things, but I get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about paying for Aarav's studies. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a separate account now, 300 a month, and talk to him about a trade or a practical degree like accounting or health. I won't push him into something I can't afford if jobs vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time mean for you compared with the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra time means I can go slowly, and slow is how I do things. In the 2028 picture I'd be running, but with five years I can walk, and I'd arrive in better shape.

say: I'd say five years is time to prepare, and I'd offer to train younger staff in **talking to customers**.
At the temple I'd say work hard and save.
think: I'd have time to adjust, but I wouldn't know **to what**.
At 48, I'd worry about paying for **Aarav's** studies.
do: Build the side business selling **rice and spices** to a few restaurants.
Save **600 a month**, with Vikram's income and mine in different baskets.
feel: **Steadier than 2028**: five years is enough to learn a new thing slowly.
S3.quote: In the 2028 picture I'd be running, but with five years I can walk, and I'd arrive in better shape.
fieldNote: Tara frames time as **pace**: slow is how she learns, so five years helps her more than most.
Opens a separate account for her son's studies and prefers practical, hard-to-automate fields.
Still anxious because her desk role would be gone by the end of the five years.

steps.text: Build a side business selling rice and spices to restaurants
Take a bookkeeping course in the evenings
Save 600 a month in a separate account
Open a 300 a month account for Aarav's studies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a generation of work, so let's train our young ones properly. At the temple I'd say plan for your children, not just yourselves. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I could get through it. I'd be 53, the mortgage finished, the children grown or nearly, and I'd have time to learn slowly. My worry would be Aarav and Diya, entering the work world when thinking jobs are the ones going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and get to know the tools in small steps, with the patient person beside me I mentioned. I'd keep the side business small but real. And I'd put 400 a month toward the children's studies and aim for practical subjects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. I'd say it feels like a long road with a few bends. I'd keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep the side business small but real. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One or two restaurant customers, supplying their rice, oil and spices, with Vikram doing the deliveries on Saturdays. It would bring in about 400 a month, and give me something of my own that doesn't depend on Hartley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children Aarav and Diya to know in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children Aarav and Diya to know how to work with people, how to be honest, and how to earn a living with something they can touch. Machines can't give that to them, and I'd want them to have it.

say: I'd say ten years is a **generation of work**, so train the young ones properly.
At the temple I'd say plan for your children, not just yourselves.
think: I could get through it: at 53 the **mortgage** would be done.
My worry is **Aarav and Diya** entering work when thinking jobs are the ones going.
do: Learn the tools in **small steps** with a patient colleague beside me.
Keep a small **side business** supplying one or two restaurants.
Put **400 a month** toward the children's studies, aiming at practical subjects.
feel: **Fairly calm**: a long road with a few bends.
S4.quote: I'd want my children Aarav and Diya to know how to work with people, how to be honest, and how to earn a living with something they can touch.
fieldNote: Tara's tone shifts from **self-protection** to protecting her children's future.
The side business is small by design: about 400 a month and independent of Hartley.
Values honesty, people skills and touchable work as things machines can't give.

steps.text: Learn the tools in small steps with a patient colleague
Keep a small side business supplying one or two restaurants
Put 400 a month toward the children's practical studies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because two years leaves no time for someone like me to learn slowly. What would help is notice, a patient course in work hours, and a family firm that says out loud who it will keep. I'd also like local help, like the temple and the council, ready for families who lose a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: People who don't like new things aren't foolish. We're careful because we've seen what happens when everyone rushes. Give us time and a person to learn from, and we get there.

headlineQuote: People who don't like new things aren't foolish. We're careful because we've seen what happens when everyone rushes.
portrait: Tara is a **43-year-old buyer** of groceries for a family wholesaler, with a husband, two children and deep roots in her community.
She is traditional, favours work and family over handouts, and has **never used AI tools**.
Her calm rests on relationships and the owner's loyalty, and it cracks as the warning time shrinks.
She would ask family and the **temple** for help only for her children's sake.
She prefers slow learning with a patient person, a small side business and practical studies for her children.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, because two years is too short for a slow learner.
whatWouldHelp: Early notice, a **patient course** in work hours, and a firm that says who it will keep.
